h1: Sabro hops and the coconut note they bring to an IPA
title: Sabro Hops: Coconut Aroma in an IPA | Craft Beer School
desc: What Sabro hops taste like, why they smell of coconut and tangerine, plus how to dose them in a 20 litre IPA without it turning into suncream.
teaser: Sabro smells of coconut, tangerine and a little mint. A small charge is a delight. A large one is suncream.
standfirst: Sabro is an American hop with an aroma few brewers expected from a hop: coconut, backed by tangerine and stone fruit. Here is how to use it in a home IPA without letting the coconut take over.
sections: An American hop that smells of coconut

Sabro came out of the Hop Breeding Company in the Yakima Valley and reached brewers in the late 2010s. It is a high alpha, dual purpose variety, with alpha acids usually in the low to mid teens. Its fame, though, is aroma.

Most American hops lean on citrus, pine or resin. Sabro adds a creamy coconut note with tangerine, ripe stone fruit and a trace of mint or cedar underneath. Tasters disagree about the proportions from lot to lot, so treat any description as a starting point rather than a promise.
Why it behaves differently from a citrus hop

The coconut character sits in the hop oil, so it is a late hop story. Boiled for an hour, it largely vanishes and you are left with plain bitterness. Added at whirlpool or in the dry hop, the oils survive and the aroma shows.

It is also a hop that rewards restraint. In a trial we would run on any new hop, a small dry hop of around 3 g per litre gives a coconut lift that sits comfortably inside an IPA. Push towards 8 g per litre and the beer reads as sweet and creamy in a way that tires the palate by the second glass.
A 20 litre hazy pale ale to learn it on

For 20 litres with an original gravity near 1.060, use 80% pale malt, 12% flaked oats and 8% wheat malt. Bitter lightly to about 25 IBU from a neutral hop in the kettle. A 60 minute addition of a 12% alpha hop at 28% utilisation needs 25 x 20 / (0.12 x 0.28 x 1,000) = 15 g. Leave Sabro for later.

  • Whirlpool at 75 to 80 °C for 20 minutes: 40 g of Sabro.
  • Dry hop on day three of fermentation: 40 g of Sabro.
  • Second dry hop after fermentation: 40 g of Sabro, with 20 g of a citrus hop.

That is 120 g of Sabro in total, or 6 g per litre. If it is your first batch, cut it to 4 g per litre and taste before you scale up.

Coconut and tangerine need something to stand on. A clean base of pale malt and a little oats keeps the hop in front. Avoid heavy crystal malt: caramel sweetness plus coconut turns the beer into dessert.

For hop partners, pick ones that add structure rather than competing sweetness. Chinook brings pine and a dry finish. Azacca pushes the fruit towards mango. Polaris shares Sabro's minty side, so use the two together carefully or the beer starts to taste of toothpaste.
Yeast, temperature and the cold chain

A neutral American ale yeast fermented at 18 to 19 °C lets the hop speak for itself. A fruity English-derived strain will add peach and apricot esters that blur where the hop ends and the yeast begins. Neither is wrong. Decide which beer you want before you pick the yeast.

Hop aroma is the first thing to go in heat. A hop forward beer carried across an Indian summer in a warm car will lose its coconut within a couple of weeks. What remains tastes flat and bready. Keep finished beer at 2 to 4 °C from the day you package it. Drink it young.
Reading the aroma before you brew

Pellets from the same variety can smell different from one pack to the next. Before you commit 120 g to a batch, tear open the pack and smell a pinch. Rub a few pellets between warm palms and sniff. You want tangerine, coconut and something creamy. If you smell hay or cheese, the hop is old or has been stored warm. No recipe will fix that.

Do the same with a hop tea. Steep 2 g of pellets in 200 ml of hot water for five minutes, cover the cup and smell it once it cools to drinking temperature. The tea shows you roughly what the hop will give in a whirlpool and which notes to keep or cut. It costs almost nothing and can save a batch.

Brew the same recipe twice, once with Sabro alone and once with half Sabro and half Chinook. Pour both blind for a friend and ask which one they want a second glass of. That is a better test of dose than any chart. If you want to understand why coconut aroma fades faster than pine, or how oxygen and yeast change hop oils, that is the kind of question we work through in the Advanced Brewing Science course.
faqs: Coconut, tangerine and stone fruit, with hints of mint or cedar. The balance changes from lot to lot.
It can bitter, because alpha acids are high. Most brewers save it for the whirlpool and dry hop, where the coconut aroma survives.
How much Sabro should I use in a 20 litre batch?
Start near 4 g per litre across the whirlpool and dry hop, which is about 80 g. Raise it only after tasting. Past 8 g per litre the coconut tends to dominate.
